messages.subject: [statnet_help] Geographic distance in ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a social network "net". Each edge has an attribute "distance"
indicating the geographic distance (in meters) separating the two actors:

  network::list.edge.attributes(net)
  [1] "distance"

The summary of the vector "distance" is

  Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.  Max.
  0    21820   155100   338200   483300 17010000

How should I specify the model to measure the significance of 'distance' in
the formation of edges?

Is this correct?

  ergm(net ~ edges + edgecov(net, attr='distance'))

(It seems to me this formula provides counterintuitive results, with the
coefficient for distance being positive)

Thanks

Francesco

e: francesco.bailo@sydney.edu.au <francesco.bailo@uni.sydney.edu.au>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Geographic distance in ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Francesco.  This is because you are only considering the distance 
between nodes that have ties - non-adjacent dyads are being treated as 
co-located (i.e., distance 0).  That will indeed produce a positive 
"effect" of distance under propinquity.  Instead, what you want to do is 
produce an n x n distance matrix and pass that to edgecov; in typical 
use cases I would suggest using the log distance, as this approximates a 
power law SIF (see e.g. Butts and Acton (2011) for a description of SIFs 
and the difference they make for network structure).

Hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] how to combine several networks
messages.body_plain:
Got another question:

I'm currently creating several independent, egocentric-type networks. I 
know that some individuals show up in more than one of these 
"independent" networks and I would like to now link the networks 
together. I already have code that does the merging of individuals (i.e. 
if person X and Y turn out to be the same, I combine them and their 
connections into 1 person).

What I can't figure out is how to take 2 networks and combine them into 
one large one. I. e. something like Nlarge = N1 + N2, where Nlarge 
consists of 2 (initially disconnected) networks with N1+N2 edges and 
N1+N2 vertices. It seems like it should be simple, but I just can't find 
a command in the various statnet packages that seems to do the job.

N1 and N2 have exactly the same structure, all edges and vertices have 
the same attributes, etc. I think I could do it by turning one network 
into an edgelist and adding to the other, but then I would loose all my 
many edge and vertex attributes.

Thanks!
Andreas


P.S.: Thanks for the answers to my last post.

-- 
Andreas Handel
Assistant Professor
Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics
College of Public Health, University of Georgia
Athens, Georgia 30602, USA
http://handelgroup.uga.edu/

messages.subject: [statnet_help] how to combine several networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Andreas -

If the alters are labeled, and if individuals can appear more than once 
across the ego nets, then these are not independent networks.  There is 
no single command to combine these into one aggregate network, but one 
reasonable strategy would be as follows:

1. Use network.initialize to create an empty graph of the appropriate 
size, with such vertex attributes as are appropriate. (These can also be 
added later.)

2. Use a for loop to walk through your list of individual networks, 
extracting and adding the edges from each one to their appropriate 
places in the master network using e.g. add.edges or the assignment 
operator.  (If you have edge attributes, these may be added at this time 
via the additional arguments to add.edges.)

Note that, depending on your design, some edge variables may have been 
unobserved; these should be set to NA, assuming that you intend to model 
the resulting graph using e.g. ergm().  (You will also want to take care 
that any subsequent analysis accounts for your measurement design, to 
the extent possible.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hello Andreas,

I am a fellow statnet user, not a developer, but I have an idea that might be worth trying.

I'd start by combining the node lists 'nodes.N1' and 'nodes.N2':
nodes.N <- c(nodes.N1, nodes.N2)

N <- network.initialize(nodes.N)

Then combine the edgeliststs by 'edges.N1 <-network.edgelist(N1)', and 'edges.N2 <- network.edgelist(N2)'.
edges.N <- rbind(edges.N1, edges.N2)

Add these edges to the large network N
add.edges(N, edges.N)

I think the above code should merge the two small network datasets into one large one. I'd be curious to hear if the above works.

Aditya Khanna
University of Chicago

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Memory-related question
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I have a question about initializing a network from the list of nodes, vs initializing from the list of edges. If I use the former  approach (and then use 'add.edges'), I get memory errors (I am working on a cluster with 4 nodes at UChicago and 20 K MB of RAM per node.) Starting with the edgelist, I get no such errors. This is a large Facebook network with 182998 nodes and 327741 edges.

Both versions of my code, one that initializes the network from the nodelist, and the second that initializes from an edgelist are available at: https://gist.github.com/khanna7/8cc8fea08e8b81066c67

Is it possible that initializing from nodes somehow requires more memory? I often prefer this approach because I find that sometimes initializing from the edgelist leads to isolates being excluded from the network.

Thanks,
Aditya

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Memory-related question
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Aditya -

Your second method of network creation can indeed omit isolates 
(specifically, it uses the maximum observed vertex ID as the number of 
vertices unless an "n" attribute is present), so the first method might 
result in a larger object.  Also, you did not in the second case 
indicate that the graph should be undirected (so the two objects will 
not be equivalent).  However, neither approach should produce memory 
errors if the data is well-formed. My guess is that there is something 
glitchy in the edgelist; add.edges will try to catch things that would 
produce issues, but some things can get past the default checks.  Can 
you verify that the values of fb.edge.list are integers denoting vertex 
IDs, that these IDs are all within the range 
1,...,length(full.node.list)? Since this is a simple graph, you will 
want to also verify that each unordered pair appears only once and that 
there are no loops.  You can also check the resulting object by coercing 
it back to an edgelist and verifying that it matches your data.  (The 
summary command should likewise show the correct number of vertices and 
edges.)

The other possibility is that your network objects are fine, and that 
your errors have to do with what you are doing downstream. But I would 
verify the objects first.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Questions on 'cug.test' with FUN=centralization
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Thank you in advance for your help with a first-time poster's questions!

I recently ran some 'cug.test's with 'FUN=centralization', and I had
questions about the output p-values not adding up to 1 and the
'ignore.eval' argument possibly being reversed (in the sense of what it
does when given 'TRUE' vs 'FALSE').

Pasted below are two runs on a dataset and the results from each, and the
network (n2014) is attached. Please let me know if the attachment doesn't
work.

First, you can see clearly that  Pr(X>=Obs) +  Pr(X<=Obs) is much larger
than 1 (0.30985 + 0.8965 = 1.20635). This seems like a bigger difference
than should happen due to rounding or very small numbers. The numbers were
even larger for some other datasets I tested.

Second, I did several analyses with both 'ignore.eval=FALSE' and
'ignore.eval=TRUE', and after much checking and head-scratching, I have to
ask if these are logicals are actually reversed? If I understand correctly,
'ignore.eval=TRUE', the default, should run the analysis on a binary
version of the network. Yet setting 'ignore.eval=FALSE' (supposed to turn
on edge weights) gives the same output as running the analysis on the
actual binary version of the network.

Any insight you all have would be much appreciated. Thank you!

Cheers,
Tina


c2014.out <- cug.test (dat = n2014   # input graph(s)
                       , FUN = centralization
                       , mode = c("digraph")
                       , cmode = c("edges")
                       , reps = 20000
                       , ignore.eval = FALSE  ## IS THIS REVERSEd?
                                          , FUN.args = list(degree,
cmode="outdegree")
)
c2014.out
# Conditioning Method: edges
# Graph Type: digraph
# Diagonal Used: FALSE
# Replications: 20000
#
# Observed Value: 0.1574074
# Pr(X>=Obs): 0.30985
# Pr(X<=Obs): 0.8965

c2014.out2 <- cug.test (dat = n2014   # input graph(s)
                        , FUN = centralization
                        , mode = c("digraph")
                        , cmode = c("edges")
                        , reps = 20000   # number of Monte Carlo reps to use
                        , ignore.eval = TRUE    ## IS THIS REVERSEd?
                        , FUN.args = list(degree, cmode="outdegree")
)
c2014.out2
# Conditioning Method: edges
# Graph Type: digraph
# Diagonal Used: FALSE
# Replications: 20000
#
# Observed Value: 0.3564815
# Pr(X>=Obs): 5e-05
# Pr(X<=Obs): 1



-- 

Tina W. Wey
Postdoctoral researcher
New Mexico State University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Questions on 'cug.test' with FUN=centralization
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Tina -

The sum of Pr(X>=Obs) and Pr(X<=Obs) can certainly be greater than 1; 
indeed, Pr(X==Obs)=Pr(X>=Obs)+Pr(X<=Obs)-1. Depending on your network, 
the properties of the measure you are using, etc., you may find the 
probability of observing your exact GLI value under your chosen null 
model to be quite large.  (It can be important to take this into account 
when comparing results across graphs; see Butts (2011, "Bayesian 
Meta-Analysis of Social Network Data via Conditional Uniform Graph 
Quantiles" for one approach to dealing with the issue.)  If you want to 
examine the discreteness of the distribution, examining the replicate 
statistics (stored in the $rep.stat element of the list returned by 
cug.test) can prove useful.

As far as ignore.eval, note that you need to pass this to the degree and 
centralization routines as well.  Adding it to FUN.args is necessary to 
avoid getting the default behavior from centralization() (and the 
centrality function it calls).  Note that whatever function you call in 
FUN may or may not respect edge values, so this is something you will 
want to check.  At any rate, I just ran a test and the argument seems to 
be working fine - just remember that ignore.eval has to be manually 
passed to the downstream function with FUN.args.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
I?m curious if anyone has used ERGMs for a clickstream-type internet
analysis of users or otherwise has any thoughts on such an approach.  I'm
searching for patterns in a set of internet links, where each link details
transitions from one page to another and each page has a set of
characteristics.  My data are a directed edgelist form.  Here?s a greatly
simplified example (a person finds a camp site and then decides to go with
a hotel instead and checks the hotel ratings):



From, To, FromType, ToType

Home, Campsites, StartPage, LocationOutdoors

Campsites, TentSites, LocationOutdoors, LocationTent

TentSites, Home, LocationTent, StartPage

Home, Hotels, StartPage, LocationLodging

Hotels, Ratings, LocationLodging, Ratings

?



The full dataset has hundreds to thousands of rows per user, and there are
several different users with users classified by experience level.



I?d like to be able to say that users having certain characteristics tend
to follow certain types of link-click paths as they use the web site.  It
would also be nice to have an estimate on the next most likely links.  In
other words, both to characterize (and compare) general user patterns and
to try predicting the next moves.


I'm not looking for someone to do the work for me, but rather seeking
advice and (if it exists) examples of using ERGMs for such a thing.  I've
seen the Keegan paper on Wikipedia coauthorship.  That's not what I need,
but kind of gets at the same thing.



I?ll be away from internet access soon, so I might not get to followup
questions for a week or so.



Regards, Zachary

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet developers,

I have a problem regarding a statistical interaction effect which I
would like to model using an ERGM. My network contains the interactions
of politicians on an online discussion website. I have both the
politicians' party affiliation, and their position in an "ideological
space", i.e. a 2D-space spanned by left-right and liberal-conservative
political attitude. From the latter, I can compute a n x n matrix of
ideological distance between politicians. I suspected that there is a
homophily effect both for party affiliation and political distance, and
modelled this thusly:

Network ~ edges + nodematch("party") + edgecov(IdeologicalDistanceMatrix)

However, I also suspect that the effect of ideological distance is
different for dyads where both politicians belong to the same party than
for politicians of different parties (I think that ideological distance
matters more with regard to party outsiders than fellow members). I
thought that I could model this with an interaction term between
nodematch("party") and  edgecov(IdeologicalDistanceMatrix). However,
this doesn't seem to be possible with statnet ergm. Is there a workaround?

Thank you very much in advance!

Simon Schweighofer

PhD Student in Systems Design at ETH Zurich

messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,

Create a matrix containing the party nodematch term (manually, e.g., by 
having 1 entries where the row and column nodes have the same party and 
0 otherwise), multiply it with the ideological distance matrix, and 
include that interaction matrix in an edgecov term.

Philip

Am 24.07.2015 um 17:02 schrieb Simon Schweighofer:
>
> Dear statnet developers,
>
> I have a problem regarding a statistical interaction effect which I
> would like to model using an ERGM. My network contains the interactions
> of politicians on an online discussion website. I have both the
> politicians' party affiliation, and their position in an "ideological
> space", i.e. a 2D-space spanned by left-right and liberal-conservative
> political attitude. From the latter, I can compute a n x n matrix of
> ideological distance between politicians. I suspected that there is a
> homophily effect both for party affiliation and political distance, and
> modelled this thusly:
>
> Network ~ edges + nodematch("party") + edgecov(IdeologicalDistanceMatrix)
>
> However, I also suspect that the effect of ideological distance is
> different for dyads where both politicians belong to the same party than
> for politicians of different parties (I think that ideological distance
> matters more with regard to party outsiders than fellow members). I
> thought that I could model this with an interaction term between
> nodematch("party") and  edgecov(IdeologicalDistanceMatrix). However,
> this doesn't seem to be possible with statnet ergm. Is there a workaround?
>
> Thank you very much in advance!
>
> Simon Schweighofer
>
> PhD Student in Systems Design at ETH Zurich
>
>
>
> _______________________________________________
> statnet_help mailing list
> statnet_help@u.washington.edu
> http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/statnet_help

messages.subject: [statnet_help] latentnet: error with tofit="mle"
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am having troubles in fitting models with latetnent using MLE.

My network has 61 nodes (countries) and 187 edges (heroin trade between countries). The edge weights refer to the kilos of heroin traded between two countries, and they range from 6.99 to 244,020.28 (mean=4,400.69, sd=21,644.70).

Before modelling the weighted network, I am using latentnet to fit a binary logit model for whether heroin trade is 0 or >0.

My covariates include both nodal attribute effects (e.g. the number of consumers in the importing country) and relational attribute effects (e.g. the distance between countries' capitals expressed in kilometers).

I run the model including geographic distance and excluding random or latent effects, and set tofit="mle":

mymodel <- ergmm (heroin ~ absdiff ("tradePrice") + nodeicov ("consumers") + nodeicov ("seizureRate") + nodeicov ("police") + edgecov (distw, attrname = "kilometers"), tofit = "mle", verbose = TRUE)
summary(mymodel)

and I get this message:

Warning messages:
1: In sqrt(1/diag(V)) : NaNs produced
2: In cov2cor(beta.cov) :
  diag(.) had 0 or NA entries; non-finite result is doubtful
3: In sqrt(diag(mle[["cov"]])) : NaNs produced
4: In sqrt(diag(mle[["cov"]])) : NaNs produced

Can anyone help me understand what is the problem and how should I fix it?

Thank you in advance!

Giulia

--
